title: Magellanic gemstone in the southern sky [NGC 265]
caption: The open star cluster NGC 265, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 265 · constellation Tucana · about 200000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: European Space Agency & NASA Acknowledgements: Davide De Martin (ESA/Hubble) and Edward W. Olszewski (University of Arizona, USA)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A myriad of stars appears in crisp detail in this Hubble image of NGC 265, which ESA/Hubble describes as the most detailed image of the cluster to date. It was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

NGC 265 is an open star cluster, a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Unlike the dense, ancient globular clusters, open clusters are usually younger and more spread out, and over time their members drift apart.

This one lies in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way, about 200,000 light-years away. It measures roughly 65 light-years across. At such a distance, separating the stars of a cluster from one another is a challenge, and Hubble's sharp vision is what makes a view this clear possible. Studying clusters in a neighboring galaxy lets astronomers compare how stars form there with how they form in our own.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.41 x 1.41 arcminutes) and distance (200000 light years), the frame spans roughly 82 × 82 light-years. Its light set out about 200,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through blue, visual and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in a cluster in another galaxy.
